stem: A factory has two machines M1 and M2. M1 produces 60% of all items and M2 produces the remaining 40%. The defect rate for M1 is 2% and for M2 is 5%. An item selected at random from the day's output is found to be defective. What is the probability that it was produced by M1?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Computing P(M2|D) = 0.020/0.032 = 5/8 instead of P(M1|D), reversing the target machine.
Ignoring the defect rates and using only the production shares: P(M1) = 0.60 = 3/5, treating production share alone as the posterior.
Computing only the prior weighted defect numerator over incorrect total: 0.012 / (0.012+0.030) = 0.012/0.042 = 2/7, using 3% as M2 defect rate instead of 5%.

explanation_sections.punchline: Even though M1 makes 60% of items, its lower defect rate means only 3 in 8 defectives come from it.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: Bayes theorem with two hypotheses. Compute the joint probabilities: P(M1 and D) = 0.60*0.02 = 0.012; P(M2 and D) = 0.40*0.05 = 0.020. Total P(D) = 0.032. Posterior = 0.012/0.032 = 3/8.
explanation_sections.lesson: Bayes theorem re-weights prior probabilities by the likelihood of the observed outcome under each hypothesis.
explanation_sections.timing: 80 seconds. Compute both joint probabilities first, sum them for the denominator, then divide. The trap is stopping at P(M1)=0.6 or reversing to P(M2|D).
